contributions.headingText:
Normal breast and salivary glands share a similar architecture (both are tubuloacinar glands) and a similar cellular composition (both consist of luminal epithelial cells surrounded by myoepithelial cells). Furthermore, the breast can contain lobules showing pure acinar differentiation {19207954}, similar to the serous acinar cells seen in the salivary glands. The luminal epithelial cells of both glands have a similar immunoprofile, expressing low-molecular-weight cytokeratins, ER, PR, and AR. These similarities in structure result in the development of similar neoplastic lesions.

The breast can develop the entire range of tumour types encountered in the salivary glands. These salivary gland–type breast tumours share the morphological features and often the molecular alterations found in their salivary gland counterparts, but their clinical behaviour is often different. Salivary gland–type breast tumours are often triple-negative, lacking ER/PR expression and ERBB2 (HER2) amplification, but they show low or intermediate aggressive potential {20306833; 28736315}. Therefore, knowledge of their site-specific behaviour is important for correct management and avoidance of overtreatment.
